---
id: graphic-design-adjust-line-spacing
type: pattern
title: Adjust Line Spacing
summary: Set the interval between lines to support the reading task, separating lines enough to follow while keeping connected text cohesive.
status: published
verses: [graphic-design]
attribution: Original Patternverse article and fictional design examples. Existing generated photographs are reused unchanged; typography is composed separately. Only the designated baseline intervals and consequent line positions change. No reader-performance measurements are claimed.
---

The studio journal looks inviting until you reach the paragraph. Its letters are large enough and its column is reasonable, but the lines sit close together. The block forms a dense patch beneath the photograph. On a care card nearby, generous spacing creates the opposite problem: one paragraph looks like four unrelated strips.

Neither problem requires a new typeface or shorter copy. The designer needs to adjust the distance between lines.

**Adjust Line Spacing** belongs to **Typography → Readability**. Choose a vertical interval that lets the reader distinguish successive lines while still recognizing connected text. Sometimes that means adding space; sometimes it means taking space away. The decision depends on the letterforms, line length, content role, and viewing conditions.

## Adjust the interval, not the letters

A **baseline** is the reference on which most letters sit. In regular typesetting, **leading** describes the interval from one baseline to the next. It is not simply the visible white gap between letters on adjacent lines: ascenders, descenders, accents, and the font’s proportions occupy some of that interval.

For example, 12-point text on a 16-point baseline interval is commonly written **12/16**. The letters remain 12 points; their baselines are 16 points apart. In the illustrations below, sizes and intervals use artwork units rather than specifying a physical print size.

Judge the setting with actual copy. A sample containing accents and descending letters can reveal problems that a line of capitals conceals. Changing typeface may also change the apparent openness at the same nominal size and interval.

For digital text, a unitless line-height multiplier can scale with each element’s own font size. MDN explains why this often avoids unexpected inheritance results. The principle remains the same: keep the letter size and the interval between lines conceptually separate. [MDN: line-height](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Properties/line-height).

## Why it helps

The reader needs both **separation** and **continuity**. More vertical separation can make successive lines easier to distinguish. Too much can make each line appear independent, weakening the paragraph’s visible cohesion. This is a relationship between marks and intervals, not an instruction to maximize white space.

USWDS recommends at least 1.5 line height for longer text while allowing tighter settings for short headings. It also advises judging the density of the resulting block. These are design guidelines, not evidence that every font and task has the same optimum. [USWDS: Line height](https://designsystem.digital.gov/components/typography/#line-height).

Line length matters too: a reader returning from the far end of a long line must find the next start. Spacing is one part of that arrangement. A very wide column may still need narrowing; increasing leading indefinitely cannot repair every measure.

The examples demonstrate controlled changes in geometry. Their effects on comfort, comprehension, or reading speed have not been tested with readers.

## Example 1: Open up crowded journal prose

**Context and goal.** Common’s studio journal introduces its shared workspace. Prospective members should read the short passage continuously, rather than treating it as a caption to skim.

![Two matching studio journal pages show a workspace photograph above six lines of prose. Before, the lines form a dense block. After, their baseline interval increases while the first baseline, line breaks, font, letter size, photograph and all other elements stay fixed.](../assets/graphic-design/leading-journal.svg "Only baseline interval changes, 23→33 units at size 22. All six lines, words, starting anchors and imagery stay fixed.")

[Full-size comparison](../assets/graphic-design/leading-journal.svg) · [Stacked narrow-screen view](../assets/graphic-design/leading-journal-mobile.svg)

**Before and diagnosis.** Six lines are set at size 22 on a baseline interval of 23: approximately 1.05 times the type size. Nothing overlaps, but the small vertical interval gives the paragraph a compressed texture. The reasonable column width and readable letter size do not remove that density.

**Specific changes.** Increase the interval to 33, or 1.5 times the type size. Keep every word and all six line breaks, including “Members bring their own tools and leave the benches ready for the next person.” Preserve the first baseline, left edge, font, weight, color, image, crop, and footer.

**After and explanation.** Each successive line moves down by an additional ten units. Across five intervals, the paragraph becomes 50 units taller. Individual lines have more separation, while their consistent width and alignment retain a recognizable block.

**Tradeoff.** The paragraph uses more vertical space and reduces the clearance above the fixed footer. It fits here; a fuller page might require a revised layout. Shrinking the type to recover those 50 units would introduce a different compromise. The tighter original might suit a compact display treatment better than this continuous reading task.

## Example 2: Bring overly loose care instructions together

**Context and goal.** Field’s mug care card contains one connected paragraph: how to wash and store the object, what to avoid, and why to keep the note. The recipient needs a compact reference.

![Two matching mug-care cards retain the same photograph and four lines of instructions. Before, a 48-unit baseline interval spreads the prose into widely separated strips. After, a 33-unit interval brings it into a more cohesive paragraph. Font size, line breaks and first baseline remain fixed.](../assets/graphic-design/leading-care-card.svg "Only baseline interval changes, 48→33 units at size 22. Copy, four lines, starting position and photograph stay fixed.")

[Full-size comparison](../assets/graphic-design/leading-care-card.svg) · [Stacked narrow-screen view](../assets/graphic-design/leading-care-card-mobile.svg)

**Before and diagnosis.** Size-22 text sits on a 48-unit interval, approximately 2.18 times its size. The wide spaces separate lines even where sentences continue across a break. “Dry before” sits at the end of one line; “storing the mug” begins the next. Their relationship has to survive a conspicuous vertical gap.

**Specific changes.** Reduce the interval to 33 while retaining the same words, four lines, column width, and first baseline. The instructions still include avoiding sudden temperature changes and direct heat. No information is removed to make the card look simpler.

**After and explanation.** The three intervals contract by 15 units each, reducing the block’s height by 45. The prose reads visually as one paragraph rather than four separately presented statements. The photograph and title have exactly the same prominence as before.

**Tradeoff and exception.** The original spacing could be useful where a reader needs room for annotations, where lines are independent entries, or where a particular reader prefers an expanded setting. The revision serves this connected paragraph; it does not establish a maximum acceptable leading for everyone.

## Example 3: Give a short headline its own spacing

**Context and goal.** Yard’s workshop poster invites passersby to consider a clay-and-print session. Its two-line title should register as one invitation before the viewer checks the date, location, and £24 price.

![Two matching workshop posters show the title Make something, followed by with your hands. Before, the title lines have a wide 91-unit baseline interval. After, the interval is 58 units. Their size, wording and first baseline stay fixed, as do the studio photograph and event details below.](../assets/graphic-design/leading-workshop-poster.svg "Only headline baseline interval changes, 91→58 units at size 52. Both lines, first baseline, supporting text and imagery stay fixed.")

[Full-size comparison](../assets/graphic-design/leading-workshop-poster.svg) · [Stacked narrow-screen view](../assets/graphic-design/leading-workshop-poster-mobile.svg)

**Before and diagnosis.** The title “Make something / with your hands.” uses a 91-unit interval at size 52, or 1.75 times the type size. This could result from extending a generous prose setting to the heading. The title is readable, but its two halves sit farther apart than this short phrase needs.

**Specific changes.** Reduce only the headline interval to 58, approximately 1.12 times its size. Preserve its line break, first baseline, letter size, and weight. Leave the three lines of event information at their original positions and spacing.

**After and explanation.** The second title line moves upward by 33 units. The phrase occupies a more unified region, followed by a larger pause before the unchanged details. This demonstrates role-specific leading: a brief display phrase can use a different interval from supporting prose.

**Tradeoff.** Tighter headlines require inspection of the actual letterforms. Different accents or descenders could need more clearance. Wide title spacing could also be intentional in a contemplative poster or a composition organized around separate phrases.

## Techniques and further comparisons

### Relate leading to type size

A ratio can keep line spacing responsive to type size. It supplies a candidate setting, not a universal optimum. Judge the resulting visible gaps with the actual letterforms, measure and role; a two-line display phrase and sustained prose need not share the same ratio.

## Common mistakes and overapplication

**Treating more space as an automatic improvement.** Increasing leading separates lines, but can also fragment connected prose. Compare the paragraph as a whole as well as individual line gaps.

**Using leading to separate paragraphs.** Leading operates within a text block. Paragraph spacing signals a boundary between blocks. Increasing every line interval to create a section break changes the wrong relationship.

**Applying one multiplier everywhere.** Body copy, headlines, captions, and compact controls have different jobs. Consistency means repeating appropriate roles, not assigning every role the same interval.

**Ignoring expansion.** On a live page, increased spacing must not cause text to disappear behind a fixed-height container or overlap a neighboring element. WCAG’s Level AA Text Spacing criterion tests adaptation to user overrides, including line height of at least 1.5 times font size, alongside paragraph, letter, and word spacing changes. It does not require those values as the authored defaults. [W3C: Text Spacing](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/text-spacing.html).

## Limits and neighboring patterns

Spacing cannot rescue illegibly small letters, poor contrast, or unclear writing. Check the actual language, output size, and reader’s needs; these English-language examples do not establish settings for every script.

- [[graphic-design-control-line-length|Control Line Length]] adjusts how much text each line carries. It should be considered alongside the vertical interval.
- [[graphic-design-match-typeface-to-context|Match Typeface to Context]] selects the letterforms whose proportions affect the apparent space between lines.
- [[graphic-design-establish-a-type-scale|Establish a Type Scale]] gives recurring roles a size vocabulary. Line spacing supplies a separate setting for each role.
- [[graphic-design-use-spacing-to-express-relationships|Establish Consistent Spacing]] coordinates repeated layout distances. Leading concerns the internal rhythm of multiline text.

## More controlled comparisons

- Relate line spacing to type size: [full-size comparison](../assets/graphic-design/proportion-material-study.svg) · [stacked view](../assets/graphic-design/proportion-material-study-mobile.svg).

Open a comparison for its stated changes and limitations; choose the stacked view for a narrow screen.

## Source notes and credits

USWDS supplies identifiable typesetting guidance; MDN documents CSS behavior; W3C explains an accessibility requirement for adaptable text. The diagnoses, chosen values, and fictional transformations are original editorial examples, not experimental findings.

Content is fictional. Reused AI-generated photographs accompany licensed Source Sans 3 Regular. These static illustrations establish neither reader outcomes, production print, responsive implementation nor complete accessibility.

id: graphic-design-group-elements-within-shared-boundaries
type: pattern
title: Group Elements Within Shared Boundaries
summary: "Enclose elements that belong to the same meaningful unit, keeping unrelated elements outside so the visible region expresses the intended membership."
status: published
verses: [graphic-design]
aliases: ["Frame the Content"]
attribution: Original Patternverse editorial consolidation. Existing fictional controlled comparisons, AI-generated photographic sources and source records retained; full caption notes archived; typography and layouts remain unchanged. No new reader study or measured improvement.
---

A studio supplier offers two tableware sets. Its sheet puts a delivery charge under the mug set, inside that set’s box. The words say “Both sets,” but the outline says something narrower. A reader checking the bowl set may skip the note or wonder whether its delivery costs something else.

The information is present. The design gives conflicting answers about where it belongs.

**Group Elements Within Shared Boundaries** belongs to **Perceptual Organization**, under common region. It uses the inside and outside of a visible region to express membership: these details form one offer, these controls answer one question, these entries belong to one category.

## Make the region describe a meaningful unit

Start by naming what the region represents: *one session*, *one delivery address*, *one offer*. Then include its necessary members and exclude details that apply elsewhere. The name should explain the grouping better than “the things that fit in this rectangle.”

A region can be established by an outline, a background panel, or another perceptible enclosure. It does not require a different color for every group. Use enough boundary to make membership clear, with clearance between content and edge; a heavy border is rarely the essential intervention.

The distinct decision here is **what shares a region**. Selecting the information units belongs to Chunk Information. Bringing their members closer is proximity. A frame can also protect text from a busy photograph or establish a page margin; those are broader framing decisions. This pattern asks whether the enclosure’s implied membership matches the message.

## Why enclosure changes the reading

Stephen Palmer’s foundational common-region paper showed that elements inside the same region can appear grouped, including demonstrations where enclosure overcomes proximity or similarity. The finding concerns perceptual grouping; it does not establish that cards always improve comprehension or that every outlined layout is preferable. [Palmer, 1992](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1516361/).

The practical consequence is that enclosure contributes information of its own. A price and a title need not sit immediately beside each other to appear part of one record when they share an enclosing region. Conversely, a note inside one offer may inherit that offer’s apparent scope even when its wording says otherwise.

McGill’s design guidance distinguishes proximity from region and illustrates region through shared outlines and background fields. That supports the technique, while the appropriate grouping still depends on the content and task. [Proximity and region](https://www.mcgill.ca/web-services/resources/toolkits/digital-design-toolkit/design-principles/proximity-and-region).

The following transformations are original editorial demonstrations. Their boundary changes are verified; their effects on readers have not been measured.

## Example 1: Make each session a complete record

**Context and goal.** Visitors pick up a programme at Yard Studio. They need to connect an activity with its room, time, price, and included materials before booking.

![Two identical photographic studio programmes show Clay bowl and Print a tote sessions. Before, the names, rooms, times, prices and inclusions have no enclosing outlines. After, one thin rectangle surrounds all the details for each session; every word and position remains unchanged.](../assets/graphic-design/boundaries-session-records.svg "Only two outlines appear, each enclosing a complete session record. Copy, typography, positions and imagery stay fixed.")

[Full-size comparison](../assets/graphic-design/boundaries-session-records.svg) · [Stacked narrow-screen view](../assets/graphic-design/boundaries-session-records-mobile.svg)

**Before and diagnosis.** The programme already has useful headings and aligned columns. A careful reader can follow it. However, the right-hand room and price details are physically separated from the activity name, and repeated treatments create a parallel column of similar-looking information. For a visitor dipping into one session, membership depends on tracking the rows and gaps correctly.

**Specific changes.** Add one thin outline around each complete record. “Clay bowl,” “Studio 1,” “10:00–12:00,” “€45 / person,” and its inclusion line share one region. The tote session gets an equivalent region. Keep the general booking line outside both because it serves the programme as a whole.

**After and explanation.** The outline supplies a continuous enclosing reference across the two columns. The intended unit is an entire session rather than a left-hand description accompanied by a separate list of logistics. No detail becomes larger or more prominent; the intervention makes its membership explicit.

**Tradeoff.** Two outlines add visual structure and make the programme feel more administrative. With only two sessions and generous separation, the original may already work well. Enclosure earns its place if visitors misassociate details or the programme needs dependable repeated records; it is unnecessary decoration if observation reveals no such need.

## Example 2: Release a shared condition from one offer

**Context and goal.** Field’s supply sheet presents a €24 mug set and a €32 bowl set. Buyers need to understand that delivery costs €6 and dispatch takes three days for either option.

![Two identical tableware sheets show a mug photograph and two priced set options. Before, the mug-set outline extends down around Both sets, Delivery €6 and Dispatch in 3 days, while the bowl-set outline ends above them. After, only the mug outline becomes shorter, leaving the shared terms outside both set regions.](../assets/graphic-design/boundaries-shared-delivery.svg "Only the left outline shortens, from 285 to 140 units. Shared terms remain in place, outside both offer boundaries.")

[Full-size comparison](../assets/graphic-design/boundaries-shared-delivery.svg) · [Stacked narrow-screen view](../assets/graphic-design/boundaries-shared-delivery-mobile.svg)

**Before and diagnosis.** The designer has extended the left box to accommodate a useful note. This is a plausible production shortcut: add new copy beneath the first offer and stretch its container. But “Both sets” is now enclosed as a member of the mug offer. The literal statement and the spatial statement disagree.

**Specific changes.** Shorten only the mug-set outline, ending it below that set’s material description. Leave the bowl-set outline untouched. Retain all three shared-term lines below the two regions, without shrinking them, moving them into a footer, or deleting them.

**After and explanation.** Each offer’s boundary now contains the same kind of information: name, price, and material. Delivery and dispatch sit outside both, consistent with their stated scope. Repairing the grouping requires less enclosure, rather than an additional box around everything.

**Tradeoff.** The shared note remains aligned to the left column, so proximity still gives it a slight association with that side. Its explicit “Both sets” label remains necessary. In a wider redesign, a shared heading spanning both columns could reinforce the scope; it is held fixed here to isolate the boundary decision. The hero photograph conveys the range’s material character, but does not show both complete sets and cannot replace product-specific imagery when buyers need it.

## Example 3: Group the thing the reader must choose

**Context and goal.** Common’s printed day-pass sheet helps a visitor choose between a shared desk and a private studio. Each offer combines a price, access hours, room type, and booking destination.

![Two identical day-pass sheets show Desk and Studio offers beneath a workspace photograph. Before, five horizontal rectangles group headings, prices, hours, room descriptions and booking labels into separate rows. After, two vertical rectangles each contain one complete offer. Text, alignment, spacing, photograph and presentation remain unchanged.](../assets/graphic-design/boundaries-offer-membership.svg "Only the boundary path changes: five horizontal attribute regions become two vertical offer regions. Text, positions, colors and imagery stay fixed.")

[Full-size comparison](../assets/graphic-design/boundaries-offer-membership.svg) · [Stacked narrow-screen view](../assets/graphic-design/boundaries-offer-membership-mobile.svg)

**Before and diagnosis.** Every attribute has its own horizontal region. This emphasizes price against price and hours against hours. That is a coherent comparison structure, but it weakens the impression that “Desk,” “€18 / day,” “09:00–18:00,” “Shared room,” and “Book desk” constitute one selectable package.

**Specific changes.** Replace the five horizontal enclosures with two vertical ones, each spanning an offer’s heading through its booking label. Keep the shared Wi-Fi and coffee statement outside both. Change no copy or layout positions.

**After and explanation.** Each complete offer becomes the enclosed unit. The eye can still compare equivalent rows because their alignment is preserved, while the boundaries emphasize what comes with each choice. This demonstrates a change in grouping logic rather than a general improvement in neatness.

**Tradeoff and exception.** If the task were to audit access-hour differences across many venues, horizontal grouping or a properly labeled comparison table might be more useful. The before is an anti-pattern only relative to the stated goal of selecting a complete offer. Neither enclosure arrangement resolves whether the reader understands the difference between a shared and private room. These are printed booking labels, not functioning controls.

## Techniques and further comparisons

### Frame the Content

An enclosure should contain the complete unit it claims to describe. A price, its inclusions and its collection arrangement may form one offer; a delivery condition shared by two offers should remain outside both local boxes. Remove redundant inner frames when the outer region already establishes the unit.

A panel used mainly to protect text over a photograph solves a different problem. See [[graphic-design-separate-figure-from-ground|Separate Figure from Ground]].

## When boxes become the problem

**Enclosing everything equally.** A box around every sentence creates many small units without explaining which belong together. Reserve separate regions for meaningful differences; use ordinary typography and spacing within them.

**Mistaking physical fit for membership.** A policy, caption, or button should not join a group merely because there is room inside its container. Check its actual scope before adjusting the outline.

**Using boundaries to excuse contradictory spacing.** If an item nearly touches a neighboring group while floating far from its own, an outline may win the grouping contest but still create tension. In finished work, coordinate enclosure and proximity rather than making them fight.

**Assuming visible grouping is sufficient online.** A drawn rectangle does not establish a programmatic relationship. W3C recommends carrying form grouping into both presentation and code, using appropriate structures such as fieldsets and legends. These static illustrations demonstrate visual membership only. [W3C: Grouping Controls](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/grouping/).

Enclosure also has limits when groups overlap. An event can belong to both “For beginners” and “Evening sessions”; two exclusive boxes may falsely imply that it belongs to only one. Labels or filters can express overlapping categories more honestly.

## Limits and neighboring patterns

A boundary expresses belonging. It cannot establish that the chosen group is meaningful, clarify ambiguous wording, or guarantee that someone notices every condition inside it. Review the grouping at the actual viewing size, and check how it survives longer copy and narrow layouts.

- [[graphic-design-chunk-information|Chunk Information]] decides which details form useful units. Enclosure makes those decisions visible.
- [[graphic-design-use-spacing-to-express-relationships|Group Related Elements Through Proximity]] expresses membership through relative distance. It may communicate the same relationship with fewer marks.
- [[graphic-design-signal-relationships-through-similarity|Signal Relationships Through Similarity]] connects categories or roles through repeated appearance, including across separate regions.
- Frame the Content establishes useful fields and scope through margins, surfaces, and boundaries. This pattern concentrates on the membership that a shared region implies.

## More controlled comparisons

- Frame the price with what it includes: [full-size comparison](../assets/graphic-design/frame-workshop-offer.svg) · [stacked view](../assets/graphic-design/frame-workshop-offer-mobile.svg).
- Frame the meaningful unit, not every line: [full-size comparison](../assets/graphic-design/frame-product-details.svg) · [stacked view](../assets/graphic-design/frame-product-details-mobile.svg).

Open a comparison for its stated changes and limitations; choose the stacked view for a narrow screen.

## Source notes and image credits

Palmer’s 1992 paper supplies the perceptual basis; McGill provides identifiable design guidance; W3C supplies the implementation distinction for forms. None evaluates these particular designs or establishes a numerical improvement in speed, comprehension, or bookings.

The organizations, offers, prices and addresses are fictional. AI-generated photographs are reused with native typography and boundaries. Checks confirm controlled differences; no audience study or physical print trial was conducted.

---
id: graphic-design-build-reusable-templates
type: pattern
title: Build Reusable Templates
summary: Define editable content roles, required information and tested layout responses so recurring materials can accept new inputs without reconstructing the design or losing meaning.
status: published
verses: [graphic-design]
attribution: Original Patternverse article and fictional data-driven template comparisons. Existing AI-generated photographs reused unchanged with separately composed native typography and layout. Three renderers each use two content inputs. Declared changes repair title capacity, conditional-offer grouping or an absent-image/long-note variant. No measured production-speed, comprehension or error-reduction result is claimed.
---

A studio copies last month’s workshop notice, replaces the title and changes the price. The new title is longer, so its last line disappears. A reduced-price condition lands beneath the booking address. Later, a monthly review inherits an old photograph because nobody supplied a new one.

The files were reusable in the narrow sense that they could be duplicated. The design had not specified how new content should behave.

**Build Reusable Templates** belongs to **Unity & Visual Systems**. Give recurring work a dependable structure: named content roles, protected relationships, editable inputs and agreed responses when content is longer, conditional or absent. Test those responses with filled examples before handing the template to another editor.

## Reuse the decisions as well as the file

A grid locates elements. A shared visual language gives them consistent roles. A template carries those decisions into a repeatable production process: what someone replaces, what must remain, and when an input needs another layout or a designer’s review.

The fictional Common programme uses three small agreements:

| Template | Required content | Defined response to variation |
|---|---|---|
| Workshop notice | Title, date, price, venue, booking address | A longer title expands its band; the image and details move together |
| Workshop offer | Session facts and price; eligibility for a reduced place | Keep a supplied condition beside its price, before the booking address |
| Monthly review | Current figures, data note and source reference | Omit an absent photograph; allow a longer note without hiding qualifications |

These agreements need not require automation. A well-labeled design file with approved variants can serve the same purpose. Separate instructions from the finished artwork, identify the current version and name who can approve exceptions. An unexplained layer called “Text copy 7” is a poor substitute for a role such as “Eligibility condition.”

## Why the structure helps

Without explicit rules, each edition reopens decisions that should already be settled. Editors improvise around inconvenient content: shrink a title, move a condition to the footer, or keep an old image to fill a gap. A template can make the appropriate response available before that workaround becomes necessary.

Adobe InDesign’s parent pages provide one implementation of reuse: repeating headers, logos, guides and other elements can be maintained across the pages that inherit them. That controls shared artwork; it does not decide which information a reduced-price offer requires. The content rules still need to be designed. [Adobe: Create and apply parent pages](https://helpx.adobe.com/indesign/desktop/create-and-organize-pages/create-and-manage-parent-pages/create-parent-pages.html).

Testing filled instances exposes a different class of problem from inspecting an empty frame. A long title reveals capacity; an absent photograph reveals fallback behavior. Victorian Government prototyping guidance recommends realistic, accurate content even in rough prototypes. These fictional inputs demonstrate those tests. [Low-fidelity prototyping](https://www.vic.gov.au/low-fidelity-prototyping).

## Example 1: Let a title change the layout without shrinking the facts

**Context and goal.** A studio administrator prepares notices for “Clay bowl” and “Hand-building a serving bowl with a folded rim.” Both need readable dates, prices and booking information on the same notice format.

![Before and after sets show the same short-title and long-title workshop notices. The short notice stays unchanged. Before, the long notice’s two-line title window hides “a folded rim.” After, the title window expands to show the third line, and its photograph and practical details move down together. All words, type sizes and photographic crops remain fixed.](../assets/graphic-design/template-variable-titles.svg "The short input stays fixed. Only the long title’s window and downstream group change, gaining/shifting 44 units; wording, type sizes, crop and notice dimensions stay fixed.")

[Full-size comparison](../assets/graphic-design/template-variable-titles.svg) · [Paired narrow-screen views](../assets/graphic-design/template-variable-titles-mobile.svg)

**Before and diagnosis.** The copied notice accommodates the short title. With the longer input, the final phrase is clipped by the fixed title window. Checking only the original notice would not reveal this failure.

**Specific changes.** Keep the 38-unit title type and all practical-information sizes. Define a two-line minimum title band with capacity for a third approved line. When that line is needed, expand the band by 44 units and move the image and details down together. The short-title notice retains its original layout.

**After and explanation.** The complete long title appears without sacrificing the €65 price, three-hour session time, venue or booking address. The response belongs to the template; an editor need not invent a smaller type treatment for this edition.

**Tradeoff.** The short notice reserves some title space, and the long notice uses more of the page’s lower area. These examples support one to three approved title lines, not arbitrary text lengths. Longer titles require another variant or review. The line breaks are supplied editorially; the demonstration is not an automatic line-breaking engine.

## Example 2: Make the qualification part of the offer

**Context and goal.** The same Clay bowl session has a €45 standard place and a €18 reduced place for students with current ID. Prospective participants need to understand which price applies to them before booking.

![Before and after sets show standard-price and reduced-price workshop offers. The standard offer is unchanged. Before, the reduced offer places its student-ID condition at the foot, beneath the booking address. After, the same two condition lines sit directly below the €18 price, and the booking address moves below them. All copy, typography and photographs remain unchanged.](../assets/graphic-design/template-conditional-offers.svg "The standard offer stays fixed. Only the reduced offer’s supplied condition and booking-address groups move; eligibility is required input, never inferred from price.")

[Full-size comparison](../assets/graphic-design/template-conditional-offers.svg) · [Paired narrow-screen views](../assets/graphic-design/template-conditional-offers-mobile.svg)

**Before and diagnosis.** The condition is present, but the template treats it as leftover footer text. The booking address intervenes between “€18 · Reduced place” and “Students with current ID only.” The editor has preserved the words while weakening their relationship.

**Specific changes.** Make eligibility a required input whenever the reduced-offer variant is selected. Place its two supplied lines immediately below the price, then place the booking address beneath them. Leave the standard offer’s arrangement unchanged.

**After and explanation.** Price and qualification become one offer unit. “Bring ID to the session” remains visible, and the action follows the information needed to judge the offer. A required field can flag missing text; it cannot establish whether the policy itself is accurate. That remains an editorial responsibility.

**Tradeoff.** The conditional offer needs more vertical room before its booking address. Forcing both offers to share every baseline would undo the repair. A longer condition needs an expanded variant, rather than smaller type or a hidden footnote.

## Example 3: Give absence and longer notes an honest layout

**Context and goal.** Common issues a monthly studio review. October has a photograph and a short note. November has no supplied photograph and needs three lines explaining provisional attendance figures.

![Before and after sets show October and November studio-review cards. October retains its photograph, figures and short note. Before, November inherits October’s photograph and clips two lines of its data note. After, November becomes a shorter text-only card showing 10 workshops, 68 of 80 places filled, all three note lines and its November source reference.](../assets/graphic-design/template-missing-image-and-notes.svg "October stays fixed. November hides the inherited photo, moves data/note/reference up 220 units, shortens the card by 220 and reveals the full note. Values remain unchanged.")

[Full-size comparison](../assets/graphic-design/template-missing-image-and-notes.svg) · [Paired narrow-screen views](../assets/graphic-design/template-missing-image-and-notes-mobile.svg)

**Before and diagnosis.** Copying October’s card leaves its photograph attached to November. The one-line note window shows only “Counts exclude drop-in sessions.” It hides that attendance totals are provisional and late entries close on 4 December. A tidy-looking card can therefore carry stale imagery and incomplete qualifications.

**Specific changes.** Define a text-only variant for an absent image. Remove the inherited photograph from view, move the data and reference upward, and shorten this digital card. Let the note window contain all three supplied lines at the same type size. Keep November’s figures—10 workshops and 68 of 80 places filled—unchanged.

**After and explanation.** Missing imagery no longer produces an implied current photograph. The qualifications travel with the figures they explain, and the shorter card acknowledges the actual content available. October continues to use the photo variant.

**Tradeoff.** The cards no longer have identical heights. A fixed-size printed report would need another arrangement within its page boundary. A missing value also needs its own policy; it must not silently inherit last month’s number or become zero.

## Keep exceptions visible

A template is overapplied when its appearance matters more than the information it carries. Automatic shrinking, unexplained clipping, stale defaults and an ever-growing collection of near-duplicate files are signs that the rules need attention.

Keep a small set of approved filled examples with the master, including difficult inputs. Record which changes are safe and which require review. Test the exported result in its intended medium, not only the editing canvas. GOV.UK’s prototyping guidance similarly distinguishes testing a realistic idea from establishing that its production implementation is ready. [Making prototypes](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/design/making-prototypes).

A bespoke composition can be appropriate for a one-off exhibition or an unfamiliar format. Reuse earns its maintenance cost when the task genuinely recurs. If exceptions dominate, reconsider the template’s scope instead of forcing every commission through it.

## Limits and neighboring patterns

- [[graphic-design-establish-a-shared-visual-language|Establish a Shared Visual Language]] defines stable visual roles and permitted variation. Templates make those roles usable in recurring production.
- [[graphic-design-establish-a-grid|Establish a Grid]] provides geometric structure. A template also defines content obligations and behavior when inputs vary.
- [[graphic-design-match-form-to-purpose|Match Form to Purpose]] determines whether the format serves the task. Faithful reuse cannot rescue an unsuitable format.
- [[graphic-design-control-line-breaks|Control Line Breaks]] shapes readable phrases within a text area. It helps prepare title inputs without replacing capacity and overflow rules.
